summary: From Caesarea Philippi on, Jesus teaches plainly that He must suffer, die and rise; He rebukes Peter and calls all who follow Him to take up their cross.
key_insight: Soon after calling Peter blessed, Jesus calls him “Satan.” The disciple who had just received the Father’s revelation now speaks for “the things of men,” urging a crown without a cross, the same path the devil had offered in the wilderness.
story: From that time Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, be killed, and be raised the third day. {Mt} He spoke this word openly. {Mk}
Then Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him: “Far be it from You, Lord; this shall not happen to You!” {Mt}

But Jesus turned around and looked at His disciples, {Mk} and He said to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are an offense to Me, for you are not mindful of the things of God, but the things of men.” {Mt}

Then He called the people to Himself along with His disciples {Mk} and said to them all, “If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow Me.” {Lk} “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and the gospel’s will save it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” {Mk}

“For whoever is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man also will be ashamed when He comes in the glory of His Father with the holy angels.” {Mk} Then, Jesus said, He will reward each according to his works. {Mt}
And He said to them, “Assuredly, I say to you that there are some standing here who will not taste death till they see the kingdom of God present with power.” {Mk}
differences: Matthew and Luke say the Son of Man will be raised “the third day”; Mark says “after three days.”
Only Matthew records Peter’s words, “Far be it from You, Lord,” and Jesus’ “You are an offense to Me.” Luke does not record Peter’s rebuke at all.
Mark says Jesus called the crowd as well as the disciples; Luke alone says the cross is to be taken up “daily.”
The closing promise varies: “the Son of Man coming in His kingdom” (Matthew), “the kingdom of God present with power” (Mark), “the kingdom of God” (Luke).

fit.question: Did Jesus say He would rise “after three days” (Mark) or “the third day” (Matthew and Luke)?

points.label: One way of speaking
points.text: Jews counted part of a day as a day. The chief priests and Pharisees quoted Jesus as saying “After three days I will rise” and then asked for a guard “until the third day” (Matthew 27:63–64). To them the two phrases meant the same.

points.label: Counted inclusively
points.text: By the usual reckoning Jesus died on Friday afternoon and rose early Sunday: part of Friday, all of Saturday and part of Sunday. Counted the Jewish way, that is three days, and Sunday is the third day.

fit.note: The writers use two common expressions for the same span of time.
fit.short: Jews counted part of a day as a day. Even Jesus’ enemies used “after three days” and “the third day” for the same span.

fit.question: Jesus said some standing there would not die before they saw the kingdom come with power. They all died long ago. What did He mean?

points.label: The Transfiguration
points.text: All three Gospels place the Transfiguration right after this saying. About a week later Peter, James and John saw the King in His glory, and Peter later wrote that they were “eyewitnesses of His majesty” (2 Peter 1:16).

points.label: The resurrection and Pentecost
points.text: Others see the kingdom coming with power when Jesus rose, was exalted and poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:32–33), within the lifetime of most who heard Him.

points.label: Judgment on Jerusalem
points.text: Others point to AD 70, when the temple fell, as a coming of the Son of Man in judgment that some of His hearers lived to see.

fit.note: Whichever is meant, each of these came within the lifetime of people standing there; nothing requires that Jesus was mistaken.
fit.short: Many see the Transfiguration; others the resurrection and Pentecost, or the fall of Jerusalem. Each came within His hearers’ lifetime.

scene.label: Elders, chief priests and scribes
scene.text: These three groups made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council in Jerusalem. Jesus names the very men who would condemn Him.

scene.label: Take up his cross
scene.text: Rome crucified rebels and slaves, and the condemned man carried his own crossbeam to the place of execution. Jews in Jesus’ day knew the sight: after a revolt around 4 BC, the Roman governor Varus crucified about two thousand men, as Josephus records.

scene.label: Life and soul
scene.text: In these sayings the words translated life and soul are the same Greek word. A person can gain everything and lose the very self that was meant to enjoy it; Luke puts it, “is himself destroyed or lost.”

witnesses.matthew: Marks a turning point with “From that time Jesus began” (16:21), the same words that opened His preaching in 4:17. Matthew alone records Peter’s protest and “You are an offense to Me,” and the promise that the Son of Man “will reward each according to his works.”
witnesses.mark: Says Jesus spoke this “openly,” and that He looked at all the disciples before rebuking Peter in their hearing. Mark alone adds “and the gospel’s” to the call to lose one’s life.
witnesses.luke: Leaves out Peter’s rebuke and moves straight from the prediction to the call. Luke alone adds that the cross is to be taken up “daily,” an everyday matter and not only a final one.

seeing.reveals: Jesus walks toward the cross with His eyes open. His “must” shows a path set by the Father, and He refuses every voice, even a loving friend’s, that would turn Him aside.
seeing.living: Peter wanted a Christ without a cross, and a discipleship without one too. Following Jesus means saying no to self, taking up the cross daily, and trusting Him with a life that looks lost. The whole world is not worth your soul.
seeing.ponder: Where are you trying to save your life in a way that could cost you your soul?

preaching.big_idea: The Christ must go to the cross, and those who follow Him must take up theirs.
outline: The disciple who must be rebuked (8:32b–33)
preaching.watch_for: Read it right after the confession. In Matthew, Peter the rock (16:18) becomes a stumbling stone, an “offense” (16:23); the man who heard from the Father now thinks “the things of men.”
